description:
I've seen numerous domestic WC Pintails, but never a wild one of natural origin.  I realize this is to be determined yet by the FL Records Committee, but I observed its behavior carefully.  It was with a couple of Mottled Ducks that were feeding actively along the shoreline at the upper (northwestern) end of Lely Resort Lake, but it was clearly watching me the whole time I observed it. I watched it swimming and in flight, and this bird acted wary, even skittish, and seemed like a naturally wild bird to me. When I approached it at first I moved slowly, but it steadily moved away. Then after a few minutes of watching it at a distance (I was never closer than about 60-70 yards), I tried a slow approach again, but this time it took flight and flew down to southern end of the Lake. Its flight was direct and strong.

I realize the most likely scenario for a wild origin bird is on FL's east coast, but I think the weather analysis provided by Steven B. Feldstein (Professor and Senior Scientist at Dept of Meteorology and Atmospheric Science; Pennsylvania State University) in the eBird report he submitted Dec 30, 2019), and also his comments posted on FL Birdbrains listserve (Jan 8 and 20, 2020) were very supportive for the potential of natural occurrence of this individual.

description:
The duck had feathers that were brown and gray overlapping one another creating a unique design. The duck had bright red-orange webbed feet and a long yellow bill. The crown of its head was a dark gray color. The duck measured to be about 20 inches. There was a noticeable black strip that started from the side of the beak and went across the duck's eye and continued horizontally. The duck's head was grayish-white in color. This duck was dabbling along the surface of the pond. 

This duck was found swimming in the freshwater pond outside my community. It was also swimming in pairs. This duck shared similar characteristics with that of a mottled duck. These ducks are commonly found in freshwater wetlands such as ponds, ditches, and marshes. These aquatic birds favor wetlands because they cool off and clean themselves by dipping their bodies in the water. This duck is distributed mainly in the peninsula of Florida as it is found to be one of the few non-migratory birds in North America. The warm temperatures and humid environments of southern Florida provide a pleasant environment for these ducks. These ducks are being watched by the Florida Wildlife Conservation because they are currently being threatened by crossbreeding with domesticated mallards. The changing landscapes of south Florida's wetland ecosystem are also threatening these birds because they thrive on the existence of these habitats.

description:
This organism is known as a Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos), a deutrerosome of the family Anatidae belonging to the Phylum: Chordata. This organism was observed at Okeeheelee Park where the organism was in a large freshwater lake near a dock during a sunny day. The organism itself was male and appeared to be 1.5-2 ft long with a wide body and long neck. Short hairs that seemed soft and plush covered the organism from the head to the body. Large wings were also present on both sides of the body, each appearing about 1.5 ft long. The organism had a black/greenish head color, small circular eyes and a flat, yellow bill (3-4 inch). At the bottom of the organisms neck is a white collar that separates the black/greenish color from the brown color present on the chest. The brown color present on the chest faded as it became gray and white on the wings and body of the organism. The legs and feet of the organism were bright orange. The legs were very thin and the feet wide with a large amount of webbing between toes.

description:
In these photos i observed two mallard ducks near the shore of the lake behind my hose. while they were near the shore i noticed they were hanging out in the shade munching on small aquatic insects as well as some small fish. the male mallard appears to have the dark green color on the back of his neck compared to the female mallard which has a dark grey/black color to it. Mallards can live in almost any wetland habitat, natural or artificial. Look for them on lakes, ponds, marshes, rivers, and coastal habitats, as well as city and suburban parks and residential backyardsThe male mallard duck, called a drake, sports a glossy green head, a white ring around its neck and a rich, chestnut-brown breast. The mottled brown female mallard looks downright dull next to the male's showy feathers.
The mallard duck's outer feathers are waterproof, thanks to oil that’s secreted from a gland near the tail. Beneath this tightly packed waterproof layer of feathers lies a soft, warm layer of feathers called down. Twice a year, mallards molt, or shed, their flight feathers, temporarily grounding the birds for several weeks until the feathers grow back.A female mallard lays up to a dozen eggs in nests on the ground near water, often in a small depression or tree hole. She lines the nest with warm down plucked from her undercoat. Soon after birth, baby ducks, called ducklings, open their eyes. A little more than a day after hatching, ducklings can run, swim, and forage for food on their own. They stay in the nest for less than a month. A group of ducklings is called a brood. Outside the nest, the brood sticks close by the mother for safety, often following behind her in a neat, single-file line.https://kids.nationalgeographic.com/animals/birds/mallard-duck/https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Mallard/id

description: I can not identify this duck! They look and sound similar to Mallards but do not have green heads, although they do exhibit sexual dimorphism where the females (I assume) look very similar to female Mallards. These organisms were spotted at Ragan Park near Ybor City in Tampa, Florida. The weather was approximately 85 degrees F with nearly zero clouds or wind. They rested on the grassy bank of a shallow, polluted pond in the middle of the park in groups of 4-5. They were approximately 1/2 meter long from beak to tail and had black head feathers, white chest feathers, a yellow bill, and light orange webbed feet. They were slow moving and clumsy, and did not appear to spend great lengths of time floating in the pond. Nearby were many other bird species including Black-Bellied Whistling ducks, Muscovy ducks, Mallards, seagulls, and ibises although the group’s of individuals were segregated. One male was seen running at full speed, chasing another male away for quite a long distance along the perimeter of the pond with its bill agape. No nest was spotted nor were juveniles. I can not identify these ducks!

description:
One of the weirdest things I've ever seen. I saw a very small bird dive, like a loon or a grebe would. When I looked at it in my binoculars, I saw a lone Mallard duckling! The next time it dove, it popped up within a flock of Canada Geese. I thought at first it had imprinted on one of them, but it didn't seem to be following any specific goose. Oddly, it would sneak up behind a goose, and then, when the goose turned around, the goose would jump in surprise (can you call it jumping if it is in the water)?

In addition to this odd behavior, I couldn't find where this duckling came from! There were 5 other Mallards on the pond. 3 of them were in an all male flock. There was one pair, but they were sleeping on the opposite end of the pond that the duckling was on. How would this pair only have one duckling, and why would they allow it to get so far away?

I also thought of the possibility that maybe someone may have dumped a domestic duckling. But the entire pond is surrounded in a high fence. It would be difficult to get over, and it seems like a lot of work when that person could have just gone to another pond.

description: Mallard

Visual Description: A small to medium sized bird, less than a foot tall. Towards the end of its body, its feathers are a darker brown, but the tips of the "tail" are white. As the feathers get closer to the front of the body, they become a lighter cream color, with small darker brown spots. In the center of the body, where the wings are located, there is a prominent whit feather on either side. The bird's head is mainly the lighter cream color, but has a black strip at the top of the head, and through the eye. Its neck is short and stout. The beak is long and flat, with a pale yellow color. It has short legs and wide feet. Both the legs and feet are orange.

Habitat: The bird was found in the urban habitat of the University of South Florida's Simmons Park. It was surrounded by other ducks, and resting in the grass near a pond. The bird can be seen all throughout the US and in Canada and Northern Mexico. It is also in Europe, Asia, and Northern Africa. https://www.britannica.com/animal/mallard

description:
The Anas platyrhynchos also known as the mallard duck comes from the Chordata phylum and is a part of the Aves class. They can be found in Asia, Europe, and North America in wetland habitats that varies from lakes, ponds, marshes, rivers, and coastal areas. Male mallards are distinct from females as a key difference between them is the male green head and bright yellow beak. Meanwhile, the female is mottled brown with orange or brown bills. They tend to dip their heads in the water but rarely dive, since they spend most of their time near the surface of water. Mallard ducks typically lay around a dozen eggs and when incubation is complete males tend to abandon the nest and join other flocks of males. They can also be classified as omnivores that tend to eat a variety of plants, insects, and crustaceans.

description: Foraging
Many mallards here, but I am looking specifically at the domestic one.

Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) ducks were observed on November 7, 2020 around 2:30 pm in Milford, Delaware. 

Mallards can be identified through behavior of dabbling and markings. The male has a green head with a yellow bill, a gray body and wings, a white ring around it’s neck, and a black rump with a white tail. The female is a brown color in varying shades with a pale orange bill with dark saddles. The male was quiet and the two females were quacking. The environment in which they were found was the Mispillion River which has a boardwalk. These ducks were fairly humanized and let me approach them for pictures. This river has plenty for the waterfowl to eat including plants, seeds, worms, snails, and other insects. A flock of Canada geese (Branta canadensis) were also observed flying overhead. I could identify them by their V-shaped formation, the noises they were making, and the white saddles on their faces. The town of Milford has plenty of rivers and ponds that attracts many waterfowl species including mallard ducks and Canada geese.

Weather: high of 74°F, low of 50°F, average of 59.07°F, and the temperature at the time was 73°F. Dewpoint of 52°F, humidity of 48%, winds coming out of the south west at 5 mph. There were 0 inches of precipitation and the conditions were fair with a nice amount of sun. 

*In picture two, I’m curious if both of these ducks are mallards as one is significantly darker than the other. Maybe the darker one is a Black Duck (Anas rubripes)?

This Mallard Duck (Anas platyrhynchos) was observed Sunday, Nov 8 at around 4:15 pm. In the back of the first picture, a female mallard can be identified by its black/brown splotchy feather patterns as well as its orange legs and feet. Another species I was able to identify was the Pekin Duck (Anas platyrhynchos domesticus) which is derived from the mallard duck. I noticed that these birds traveled together regardless of what specific species they were. Seen in the picture, there are also other types of waterfowl. I observed that all of these species were able to coexist together without much of a competition. At the time of my observation, it was 70 degrees and sunny, 39% humidity, and had very slight winds coming from the east at a little bit over .5 mph.

description: These two birds were identified as Mallards because of their spotted brown and green-gray coloring, which demonstrate the typical female and male color patterns of this species. The duck on the left was light brown with darker brown striation throughout its coat, and also had an orange beak with a brown patch on it, as is typical for female mallards. The male mallard on the left was a more brownish-gray color, with a bright green head above a ring of white feathers. It also had a more yellow-colored beak. Mallards are secondary consumers. Mallards typically breed once per year. Females lay between 9-13 eggs, which hatch after about a month of incubation and enter water very soon after hatching. The young mallards become sexually mature adults after about a year. These birds appeared to be adults, as they were both fairly large and seemed to fall within the average adult length range of the species, which is 19-25 inches. Because of the differences in coloration, the bird on the left of the photos can be identified as a female while the bird on the right was a male. Mallards can be found in habitats like wetlands, marshes, lakes, and ponds. Other organisms that may be found in these habitats include beavers, frogs, herbaceous plants, and insects. These ducks were found in a small lake within a wooded area. A potential predator of mallards is the Red fox (Vulpes vulpes) and a potential source of prey is insect larvae like that of the Common Green Darner (Anax junius).  A potential competitor of this species is the American black duck (Anas rubripes).

description: Mallards are secondary consumers, eating a wide variety of food that includes, but is not limited to vegetation, insects, worms, gastropods, and other arthropods. They have a typical duck morphology with long bodies, rounded heads, wide, flat bills, and tails that sit high, out of the water. The males are characterized by iridescent green heads and necks, while the females are brown. Both sexes have an iridescent blue patch on the wings. Breeding pairs match up as early as October and continue through March. As soon as mating occurs, the males leave and the females lay 9-13 eggs in a nest on the ground near a body of water. Ducklings hatch after 26-28 days and are lead to the water by their mother. After the breeding season, some mallards fly south to warmer areas, while others stay in the same area for the winter. They are found almost anywhere in the world and dominate in the Northern Hemisphere. They prefer wetlands with productive waters that provide the vegetation and aquatic invertebrates they feed on. One potential predator is the Bald Eagle, one potential competitor is the American Black Duck, and one potential prey is the Common Green Darner.

Mallards are secondary consumers, eating everything from gastropods to aquatic vegetation or insects. Mallards can be commonly scene eating winged insects such as the American meadow hawk. Mallards are fairly big birds who are recognizable due to there distinct call and color pattern. Their calls are loud quacks. Both male and female mallard ducks are brown, with the male having a green and black head and the female have specked brown throughout her wings. Both sexes have yellow feet. These ducks live in water, such as small lakes or ponds. Mallards lay 8 to 14 eggs at a time, with the eggs hatching after around 30 days of incubation. The baby birds fledge after around 60 days. The average lifespan for a mallard is between five and ten years. The individuals I saw were a mix of male and female adults. Mallards experience predation in the form of nest parasites, such as by the ruddy duck. A competitor for the mallard is the American black duck.

description:
Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos)

22 November 2020
Avondale Park
Denton, Denton County, Texas

There’s a small stretch of Cooper Creek that borders Avondale Park where there’s a more or less permanent pool of water year-round except in the hottest years when it, like the rest of the creek, dries up. There have been perhaps two late summers when this has happened to this permanent pool of water in the past nearly two decades. Change is constant in nature. These Mallards are first-year birds born and raised in this stretch of Cooper Creek. Two Mallard females discovered the place this past spring/summer and raised between them a total of 16 ducklings into maturity (exemplified in these images). At least this is our theory because other than this there had never been a Mallard presence at this park. One hen we dubbed, “Mama,” raised 10 ducklings. The other hen was far more suspicious and wild and did not dare get close to Humans; she successfully raised six ducklings. Sometime in late August or early September, the two hens and their broods disappeared likely to be introduced to the greater Mallard society in the region (whatever that is). But weeks later, in late October and early November and since the Mallards appeared again in the same stretch of Cooper Creek where they’d first appeared earlier in the year. These Mallards are now itinerant visitors. Thus we conclude that these are young raised here and they perhaps are in the process of colonizing a new site. Credit the pioneering pair of hens in 2020 in the midst of a pandemic no less. The Humans who frequent the park and peer into the water of Cooper Creek have taken it all in stride and for the most part have let the birds be who they are without causing them undue harm. The children of the Humans are particularly thrilled at seeing the ducks in the water. Will this new generation of Mallards on Cooper Creek at Avondale Park be mating and breeding new generations going forward? Maybe the coming spring in 2021 will tell as much.
 
This is a story that’s still developing. There are plenty of hawks especially Red-shouldered Hawks and Mississippi Kites not to mention the Red-tailed Hawks and the occasional Broad-winged Hawks that appear at particular times of the year at the park. The Red-shouldered Hawks raise their young here beside the mating pairs of Mississippi Kites in spring and summer. So they may present the Mallards with a predatory challenge. There are Common Raccoons, Virginia Opossums, and Bobcats, who especially at night may prey on the Mallards, their eggs and ducklings. Lest we forget there are different species of resident Owls who at night can be heard sending their calls from the tall trees in the immediate vicinity of the creek. But for now there is a first-generation of Mallards in the creek. And they’ve taken up their place in the natural order of things.

A view of Mama and her brood from this past June 20, 2020, can be seen here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/50382672
